name: Water fasting
lead: Water fasting, also called extended or zero-calorie fasting, is abstaining from all food and caloric drinks for 24 hours or more, usually several days, while drinking water. In looksmaxxing communities it is used as a way to lose body fat quickly, with the aim of a leaner face, a sharper jaw and cheekbone definition and, as some users put it, better-looking skin.[1][2][3] Many forum users treat it as a short reset before a muscle-building phase, so the leaner starting point makes later gains easier to see.[4]

Reviews of human trials describe prolonged fasts of 5 to 20 days as producing strong ketone elevation and weight loss of roughly 2 to 10 percent of body weight, with about two-thirds of the weight lost being lean mass and one-third fat mass, based on two studies that measured body composition.[7][23] The lead author of the 2023 Nutrition Reviews review, Krista Varady of the University of Illinois Chicago, said in a university release that her group would suggest intermittent fasting for weight management because more data exist for it.[16]

The practice sits at the extreme end of a spectrum that also includes time-restricted eating, one-meal-a-day (OMAD) eating and alternate-day fasting, which have a larger trial literature.[2][6][8] Supervised programs such as the Buchinger-style clinic fast and the water-only fast at TrueNorth Health Center in California have published observational data, and the best-known historical case is the supervised 382-day fast of Angus Barbieri in 1965 and 1966.[19][20][21] Documented risks include electrolyte disturbances, gallstones and refeeding syndrome.[1][18]

angle.text: People use extended fasts to lower body fat quickly, because facial fat loss tends to follow overall fat loss and makes bone structure more visible. Some users also describe a skin-quality benefit, and others plan a fast before starting a bulk from a lean baseline.[3][4]

paras: A water fast supplies no energy: the person drinks water, and sometimes tea, black coffee or mineral and electrolyte drinks, but eats no food. Wikipedia defines prolonged fasting (also called extended or water fasting) as a fast beyond 24 hours, typically 5 to 20 days.[1] Clinical programmes in Europe often use a modified version, the Buchinger fast, with a small daily allowance of juice and broth of about 200 to 250 kcal rather than zero.[20][22]

People pursue water fasts for several reasons: rapid fat loss, a feeling of mental clarity, religious observance, or what proponents of therapeutic fasting describe as giving the body a rest. In appearance communities the dominant motive is fat loss that shows in the face, and some forum users also hope for skin improvement.[3][5]

Metabolic changes begin about 3 to 5 hours after eating. Early in a prolonged fast gluconeogenesis is high and roughly two-thirds of early weight lost is lean tissue; later ketones replace glucose as the main fuel for the nervous system, and the fat-to-lean loss ratio is about 7:6.[1] Weight loss averages about 0.9 kg per day in week one and 0.3 kg per day by week three.[1] Sodium, potassium and magnesium fall significantly, which can cause hyponatremia, and some fasting programmes use electrolyte beverages for that reason.[1]

The 2023 narrative review found that ketone levels rose sharply and plateaued after about 5 to 8 days, that waist circumference fell by 3 to 9 cm, and that sodium and chloride dropped to just below the acceptable limit after 8 to 10 days, prompting the authors to suggest considering electrolyte supplementation.[23] Rapid early weight loss is partly water and glycogen, which is why scale weight drops faster in the first days than fat mass does.[1] On muscle, Varady said in the university release that the body needs a constant protein intake and otherwise draws on muscle.[16]

Fasting is central to many religious traditions, including Ramadan, Yom Kippur, Lent and the Nineteen Day Fast of the Baha'i Faith.[1] In the early twentieth century it was promoted by alternative-health writers such as Upton Sinclair, whose 1911 book The Fasting Cure claimed it could cure nearly all diseases; in 1932 physician Morris Fishbein listed fasting as a fad diet.[1] Linda Hazzard's strict regimens caused many patient deaths.[1]

Angus Barbieri of Tayport, Scotland, fasted from 14 June 1965 to 30 June 1966 under medical observation, starting at Maryfield Hospital in Dundee and attending outpatient checkups. He lost about 125 kg, consuming only tea, coffee, sparkling water, vitamins, electrolytes and yeast, and a 1973 report said he kept a healthy weight afterwards.[19] The Guinness Book of Records listed it as the longest on record in 1971.[19]

Therapeutic fasting for obesity was studied as early as 1915, with renewed medical interest in the 1960s, according to Wikipedia's intermittent-fasting article. The 5:2 pattern was popularised in 2012 by a BBC Horizon documentary presented by Michael Mosley.[2] Within appearance communities, water fasting appears in looksmax.org threads from at least 2019, including personal journals and guides, usually framed as a fat-loss or skin-reset tool.[3][5][10]

Two clinical traditions generate much of the published human data. The Buchinger Wilhelmi clinic at Uberlingen, Germany, runs medically supervised fasts on about 200 to 250 kcal a day. Its 2019 PLoS One study followed 1,422 adults on fasts of about 5 to 20 days: mean weight loss ranged from 3.2 kg in the 5-day group to 8.6 kg in the 20-day group, fewer than 1 percent had adverse effects, about 93 percent reported no hunger, and 84.4 percent of the 404 people with a pre-existing complaint reported improvement. The authors noted that the study was observational, had no control group and was funded by the clinic's related company.[20]

TrueNorth Health Center in Santa Rosa, California, directed by Alan Goldhamer, supervises water-only fasts of about 5 to 40 days, followed by a refeeding period of at least half the length of the fast. In a 2014 interview Goldhamer reported that about 10,000 patients had fasted there, that blood pressure fell substantially in a hypertension cohort and that no fasting-related deaths had occurred; these are the interviewee's own reports, and he stated that larger independent studies are needed.[21]

A looksmax.org guide describes the author fasting for about two years, now three days monthly, with a disclaimer that it is not medical advice.[3] Other users ask whether to choose water fasting or one meal a day, with replies about low-carbohydrate approaches.[4] A user reports a three-week fast with breaks in which fat loss was large but hair fell out heavily afterward and later regrew.[3] Another thread discusses prolonged fasts with a reply advising basics and time for skin and collagen.[5]

A 2025 thread asks whether to water fast or eat one low-carbohydrate meal a day to get lean before a lean-bulk phase, noting the poster's warehouse job would make a full fast harder.[4] A separate journal thread records one user's day-by-day fast.[10] A 2026 Hacker News post describes a personal fat-loss experiment that combined AI-chatbot guidance with water fasting, prompting a short discussion.[11]

Forum users usually combine fasting with other cutting approaches, such as OMAD, low-carbohydrate diets or appetite-reducing medications, and often plan it as a short reset before a muscle-building phase.[3][4] Shorter forms such as OMAD and time-restricted eating are popular alternatives that appear in the same threads.[4]

Varady and colleagues' 2023 review reports fasts of 5 days producing about 4 to 6 percent weight loss, 7 to 10 days about 2 to 10 percent, and 15 to 20 days about 7 to 10 percent.[16] In the few trials that followed people afterwards, metabolic improvements had disappeared 3 to 4 months later, even when much of the weight loss was kept; in one study participants regained all of the weight lost from a five-day fast within three months.[16][23] Varady advised against fasting for more than five days without medical supervision.[16][17]

The review found no serious adverse events or deaths among the included studies, with mild effects such as hunger, headache, insomnia, fatigue, dizziness and dry mouth being common.[17][23] The authors listed limitations: only eight trials, most with small samples, most without a control group, and many without follow-up.[23]

A 2024 narrative review of human trials on prolonged water fasting (5 to 20 days) found strong ketone increases, weight loss of roughly 2 to 10 percent and about two-thirds of that loss as lean mass, with the authors noting that the lean-mass loss may reflect increased muscle protein breakdown. Blood pressure fell consistently; lipid results varied; and fasting glucose, insulin and HbA1c improved in people with normal blood sugar but not in people with diabetes.[7][23] The review covered eight trials, one of them randomised.[23]

A small Slovak study had ten volunteers drink only water for 11 days followed by an 11-day regeneration diet, tracking kidney function, body weight, blood pressure and oxidative stress.[12] In the KETO-ADPKD randomized trial, 66 patients with polycystic kidney disease were assigned to a ketogenic diet, water fasting or control; both interventions produced ketosis, 85 percent of the water-fasting group rated it feasible, and the ketogenic diet group showed reductions in body fat and liver volume.[13]

Shorter patterns have more trials. A 2018 pilot of 8-hour time-restricted feeding in 23 obese adults reported weight loss, and a 2022 review found time-restricted eating produced 1 to 4 percent weight loss and improved insulin sensitivity.[6][8] A 2001 crossover study of 13 volunteers compared different pre-fast meals before a 24-hour food and water fast.[14] A 2019 randomized trial in 30 men tested a hops-based appetite suppressant during a 24-hour water-only fast.[15] A 2021 review found alternate-day fasting for 2 to 6 months lowered weight and BMI in overweight adults.[1] No studies found that assess repeated multi-day water fasts specifically for facial appearance or skin.

Refeeding syndrome, a shift in potassium, magnesium and phosphate after food is reintroduced, can be severe and can occur after about 4 to 5 days without food.[1][18] During fasting insulin falls; reintroducing food restores it, which drives cells to take up phosphate, magnesium and potassium, and abnormal heart rhythms are described as the most common cause of death.[18] Wikipedia lists higher risk in people with eating disorders, people who have eaten almost nothing for many days and people misusing appetite-suppressing drugs.[18]

Fasting can raise gallstone risk, and intermittent fasting sources advise against it in pregnancy, children, older adults and people prone to eating disorders.[1][2] Forum users report non-medical effects too, including heavy hair shedding some weeks after a long fast, followed by regrowth.[3] Some commenters in other communities describe extended fasting as risky for people with a history of disordered eating.

lore.intro: Water fasting is discussed on looksmax.org as a fast fat-loss and skin tool, with some users reporting side effects such as hair shedding.[3]

claims.claim: Water fasting strips fat faster than eating less
claims.believers: Users weighing it against OMAD say they are willing to fast for faster results, and a guide author reports regular monthly fasts.[3][4]
claims.experts: Physiology sources report that early weight lost in a prolonged fast is largely lean tissue, with fat and lean loss roughly 7:6 later on; the 2023 review found about two-thirds lean mass.[1][23]

claims.believers: One user reports heavy shedding after a three-week fast with weekly breaks, with regrowth later.[3]
claims.experts: No published studies were found on water fasting and hair loss; electrolyte and nutrient changes in prolonged fasts are documented.[1][23]

claims.believers: A looksmax.org guide author says regular fasts have been part of a long-term routine, and other users in skin-recovery threads discuss fasting alongside basics.[3][5]
claims.experts: No published trials have tested multi-day fasting for skin quality; reviewed trials focus on weight, blood pressure and blood markers.[23]

claims.claim: Water fasting before a bulk gives a leaner starting point
claims.believers: A 2025 poster plans to get as lean as possible before starting testosterone and a lean bulk, weighing a fast against OMAD.[4]
claims.experts: Reviews report that about two-thirds of weight lost in a 5 to 20 day fast is lean mass, which can include muscle, and that weight regain is common in the months after.[16][23]

claims.claim: Longer fasts give extra benefits beyond weight loss
claims.believers: Advocates of supervised water-only fasting, such as TrueNorth's Alan Goldhamer, report blood-pressure reductions and describe long fasts as giving the body conditions to heal.[21]
claims.experts: The 2023 review found blood pressure fell, but improvements in blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar returned to baseline within 3 to 4 months.[16][23]

claims.claim: A fast is safe if you are healthy
claims.believers: A guide on looksmax.org presents the fast as an intense biological process with some risk and stresses reading widely first.[3]
claims.experts: Supervised-clinic studies report few adverse events, while Wikipedia and reviews describe refeeding syndrome, electrolyte loss and gallstones, and Varady advises medical supervision beyond five days.[1][16][18][20]

card.summary: Multi-day zero-calorie fasting for fast fat loss; documented risks include refeeding syndrome and loss of lean tissue.
card.note: Refeeding syndrome can be fatal and can occur after about 4 to 5 days without food.

quick.overview:
Water fasting means no calories for a day or more. Forum users use it for rapid fat loss and say it improves skin, and some report hair shedding afterward.

Physiology sources report a large share of early weight loss is lean tissue, and studies cover shorter intermittent fasts rather than repeated extended ones.
quick.mechanism: With no intake, the body uses glycogen and then protein and fat, shifting toward ketone use for the brain over days.
quick.risks: Documented risks include electrolyte loss, gallstones and refeeding syndrome, which can be fatal. Fasting is not recommended for pregnancy, children, older adults or people prone to eating disorders.
